outcome: No answer to the general question has appeared; the field continues to produce isolated results on specific graph classes (representation numbers, recognition complexity, temporal/co-bipartite extensions, split graphs, modular decomposition) but nothing that identifies which hard graph problems generically translate to efficiently solvable word problems.
summary: The bullet is an open-ended research-programme question, not a single resolvable claim: 'which (hard) problems on graphs can be translated to words representing them and solved on words (efficiently)?' As of January 2024 the only known instance was that Maximum Clique is polynomial on word-representable graphs (because their neighborhoods are comparability graphs, on which Max Clique is polynomial) — this predates the window and is cited only as background. Searching the 2024-2026 literature on word-representable graphs turns up an active but conventional (human-authored) research area: square-free word-representations (Das et al. 2024-2025, answering a different open problem about representing graphs by square-free words), word-representability of co-bipartite graphs and split graphs, a word-representable temporal graphs extension (SAND 2025), modular decomposition characterizations, and complexity results establishing that recognizing k-word-representability is NP-complete for 3 ≤ k ≤ ⌈n/2⌉. None of these answer or narrow the general question of which hard problems admit efficient word-based algorithms; each is either a structural result about representability itself or a complexity result about recognizing representability, not a case of 'hard graph problem X can (or cannot) be efficiently solved via word representation.' No survey, digestion, or new instance was found that would count as a case of this specific bullet under the scope rule (§3.1) — the found papers are all related work in the same field, not restrictions or resolutions of this stated question. No AI system was mentioned anywhere in this literature; all identified papers are conventional human mathematical/algorithmic research (search techniques, forbidden-subgraph characterizations, combinatorial constructions). I agree with the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the Maximum Clique polynomiality result (predating the window, and re-cited in surveys) is itself 'an answer' to a case of the bullet's question, making status 'open_stale' rather than 'open' for that one instance. But the bullet asks a general, open-ended question ('which problems'), and a single pre-existing example does not close or narrow the class of problems under investigation in a way that changes what a careful person would write in this entry today; no new problem instance was resolved in the window, so 'open' with no_change_found remains the better reading.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or survey that gives a general characterization, dichotomy, or meta-result identifying a class of hard graph problems that become efficiently solvable via word representation (or proves no such general translation exists for a class), rather than another isolated case involving a specific graph family.
